In one sentence: revenue was up eight percent year on year, and the margin was down one point.
Down one point. Should my board be worried?
Half of that point was a one-off, the office move. The other half is a headwind from the exchange rate, and that one will still be there.
And next year? Everybody tells me the market is coming back.

I came up through the creative side, and for years I sat through results presentations I did not understand. What changed it was one finance director who started every meeting with a single sentence. Revenue is up eight percent year on year, the margin is down one point, and here is why. Then he told me which part was a one-off and which part would still be there next quarter. That is all I need from a CFO. I do not need every line. I need to know what happened, whether it will happen again, and what is being done about it. When a candidate for that job cannot give me those three things in plain English, I assume he cannot give them to my board either.

On a board you hear the same phrases every quarter. It is expected that the market will recover in the second half. The decline is believed to be temporary. Those sentences are not wrong, but I have learned to ask who expects it and who believes it. The finance directors I trust answer that straight away. We had the forecast reviewed by the two largest clients, and both of them confirmed the volume. That is a different sentence. It tells me the work was done and who did it. When a candidate uses the passive to hide where a number came from, I notice. When he uses it to show that somebody checked, I notice that too.
